newsitem.title: UK: Oil markets pause as funds take their gains.
newsitem.headline: Oil markets pause as funds take their gains.

text.p: World oil prices stalled on Wednesday after two days of hefty increases as institutional futures buyers took profits.
Prices moved indecisively in and out of positive territory and, combined with mixed signals from U.S. industry stock data, gave a picture of hesitant market activity.
August futures in benchmark Brent blend crude closed 12 cents firmer at $18.92 a barrel in London.
Financial funds were said to be taking the opportunity to collect some gains after buying back into oil futures following a sharp fall in crude prices in June.
August Brent paper had jumped 33 and 30 cents on Monday and Tuesday after physical crude markets tightened on news that Iraq would not be resuming oil exports for some weeks.
Oil has now recovered from a 15-month low hit in June when Brent touched $17.32, having suffered a $7 slide in the space of six months.

Early losses were triggered by statistics from the American Petroleum Institute, which are closely watched by the oil industry as an indicator of demand in the world's largest crude and oil product market.
API data showed 4.36 million barrels less crude held in primary storage for the week ending June 27 and a fall in gasoline stocks of 1.23 million barrels.

The initial reaction by analysts was one of disappointment as most of the drawdown appeared to be in the U.S. West Coast area, rather than in the crucial East Coast, which soaks up crude from the Atlantic Basin.
But later figures from the U.S. Department of Energy, which concurred with the API's, gave the market some heart.
Some of the bullishness implied by the statistics was said to have already been factored into oil prices so any fall in the day was not seen as overly significant.
"These are bullish API stats, but we knew they would be with all the expectation that was out there, so we are getting some profit-taking," said a dealer.

But the good news for oil prices was tempered by realisation the peak season for gasoline was almost over and the next product in the buying cycle, oil for winter heating, looks ominously well supplied.
Traditionally the world oil market is supported by heavy demand for fuel during the U.S. summer driving season, which peaks over the July 4 weekend.
"The gasoline season is now to all intents and purposes over," said Peter Gignoux, senior energy analyst at brokers Smith Barney.

From next week attention will begin to shift to heating oil, which showed a surprisingly large build of 4.02 million barrels, pushing total stocks to 117 million barrels, up 17 million barrels year-on-year.
The eventual resumption of Iraqi exports under the second tranche of its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations will also depress prices.

When the Iraqi oil does reappear it could pour out at a rate of a million barrels per day, up from some 660,000 bpd in the first phase of the oil sale which ended in June. The heavier flow will weigh on oil markets in the Autumn.
The July 4 weekend was also expected to dampen oil market activity, with U.S. traders winding up their week early on Thursday to head to beaches and holiday homes.
